Ayrıca: {source:6:45} zulmeden kavmin kökünün kesilmesinin ardından gelen aynı söz; {source:39:73} Rablerinden sakınanların cennete bölük bölük götürülmesi ve bekçilerin selamı; {source:39:69} aynı hüküm sahnesinin başı: yerin Rabbinin nuruyla aydınlanması ve hakla hüküm verilmesi; {source:37:181} kapanıştaki hamddan hemen önce elçilere selam; {source:45:36} Câsiye suresinin bir hüküm sahnesinden sonra hamd ile kapanması; {source:35:34} cennettekilerin hüznü gideren Allah'a hamdı; {source:7:43} cennettekilerin kendilerini yola iletene hamdı

Araplar bir kimsenin çabasıyla varabileceği en uç noktaya da bu kökten bir ad verirlerdi: {ar:حماداك أن تفعل كذا أي غايتك وفعلك المحمود, tr:hamâdâke en tef'ale kezâ, ey gâyetüke ve fi'lüke'l-mahmûd, gloss:senin varabileceğin en ileri nokta şunu yapmaktır, yani son hedefin ve övülecek işin, source:"ح م د,B004"}. Bir başka açıklama şöyleydi: {ar:حماداك في معنى قصاراك, tr:hamâdâke fî ma'nâ kusârâke, gloss:hamâdâk, elinden gelebilecek en son şey demektir, source:"ح م د,B004"}. Hamdın kökü varılabilecek son sınıra ad verir. Kur'an da hamd cümlesini işlerin bu son sınıra vardığı anlarda söyletir: bir hükmün ardından, bir hikâyenin sonunda, cennettekilerin son sözü olarak. Bir başka ayet bunu açıkça söyler: {ar:لَهُ ٱلْحَمْدُ فِى ٱلْأُولَىٰ وَٱلْءَاخِرَةِ, tr:lehü'l-hamdü fi'l-ûlâ ve'l-âhira, gloss:dünyada da ahirette de hamd O'nundur, source:28:70}.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=31 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:34:1} ahirette de hamdın O'na ait oluşu; {source:53:42} son varışın Rabbe olması; {source:79:44} Kıyamet saatinin son noktasının Rabbe varması; {source:75:30} o gün sürülüşün Rabbe olması

Fâtiha ise bu sonu başa koyar. Hamd normalde bir deneyimden sonra verilen onaydır. Bir toprak içinde yaşandıktan, bir kişi sınandıktan sonra söylenir. Okuyan ise onu altıncı ayette yol istemeden önce, yolun daha başındayken söyler. Bu onayın dayanağı, ikinci ayetin kendi son kelimesindedir. Âlemler, Rabbin kendileriyle tanındığı işaretlerdir. Yol henüz yürünmemiştir, ama işaretler görülmüştür. Kur'an'ın bir hükümden sonra "denildi" diye aktardığı söz, Fâtiha'yı okuyanın ağzında, Allah'ın adından hemen sonra gelen ilk sözdür.


<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=32 kind=prose ref=7:43 -->
Cennettekilerin hamdı da yol üzerine bir sözdür. A'râf suresinde göğüslerindeki kin sökülüp alınır, altlarından ırmaklar akar ve şöyle derler: {ar:ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِى هَدَىٰنَا لِهَٰذَا وَمَا كُنَّا لِنَهْتَدِىَ لَوْلَآ أَنْ هَدَىٰنَا ٱللَّهُ, tr:el-hamdü lillâhillezî hedânâ li-hâzâ ve mâ künnâ li-nehtediye lev lâ en hedânallâh, gloss:bizi buna ileten Allah'a hamd olsun; Allah bizi iletmeseydi biz yolu bulamazdık, source:7:43}. Yolun sonunda söylenen bu hamdın konusu, altıncı ayette istenecek olan "hidâyet"in ta kendisidir.

Bu sözü söyleyenin adı geçmez. Fiil edilgendir, "denildi". Bu, Fâtiha'daki öznesiz cümlenin aynısıdır. Hüküm verilmiştir ve hamd, kimin ağzından çıktığı söylenmeden yerini bulur. Zulmeden kavmin kökünün kesildiği hikâye de, yukarıda görüldüğü gibi, aynı sözle biter.

strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.65.2	silence as praise	The commentary calls 1:2 a verb-less verdict whose praise is already located before a human says it; this psalm says silence itself is praise before God in Zion, making unspoken praise intelligible.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.148.3	sun, moon, stars	The commentary treats sun, moon, and stars as created signs rather than the Lord; this summons those same heavenly bodies to praise their Maker, giving the celestial lights a liturgical role without deifying them.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.148.7	sea and earth	The commentary says every created kind bears witness to its Lord; here the sea and its creatures, including the depths, are directly summoned into praise.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.148.10	animals	The commentary extends the Lord's care to herds and every kind of creature; this verse includes wild and domestic animals among the voices summoned to praise.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.148.11	kings and peoples	The commentary says the plural worlds include all created kinds; this verse brings rulers, nations, and peoples into the same cosmic summons to praise.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.19.2	heavens declare glory	The commentary reads each kind as a sign by which its Lord is known; the heavens here declare God's glory without a human speaker, making creation itself a witness.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.19.4	unvoiced testimony	The commentary says all things praise in a language humans do not understand; this verse says the heavens' testimony has no ordinary speech or words, closely matching praise beyond human hearing.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.19.5	voice throughout the earth	The commentary makes the created signs universal; the heavens' line and words reach the end of the world, so their testimony is not confined to one worshiping community.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.38.7	stars sing at creation	The commentary says nonhuman creation praises God before a human voice is heard; Job pictures the morning stars singing together as earth's foundations are laid.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Neh.9.6	creation kept alive	The commentary names the Lord of all worlds; Nehemiah addresses the one who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them, keeps them alive, and receives worship from heaven's host.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.43.20	wild creatures honor God	The commentary includes every kind in the Lord's domain; Isaiah says wilderness animals honor God because he supplies water in the desert.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.43.21	people formed to praise	The commentary says praise belongs to God independently of a human speaker; Isaiah says the people God formed are meant to recount his praise.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.5.13	every creature blesses God	The commentary says every thing praises God in its own way; Revelation gives a cosmic liturgy in which every creature in heaven, earth, under earth, and sea voices blessing and honor to the One on the throne and the Lamb.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.4.11	Creator worthy of glory	The commentary assigns praise to God as Lord of all worlds; the elders here give glory and honor to the one worthy because he created all things and they exist by his will.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.7	worship the maker	The commentary distinguishes the sun and moon as signs from the Lord they indicate; the angel calls people to worship the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs of water.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.17.24	Lord of heaven and earth	The commentary expands the ordinary title Rabb into Lord of all worlds; Paul calls the maker of the world and everything in it Lord of heaven and earth.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.17.25	giver, not needy recipient	The commentary says praise does not originate in human speech; Paul says God is not served as though he needed anything, since he himself gives life and breath to all.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.14.15	maker of all domains	The commentary identifies God as Lord of all worlds; Paul tells the crowd to turn from vain things to the living God who made heaven, earth, sea, and all that is in them.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.14.17	rain and food for all	The commentary develops the Rab image through cloud, water, pasture, and herd; Paul names rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness as gifts from the Creator.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.1.14	luminaries as signs	The commentary reads heavenly bodies as signs within the created world, not as its Lord; Genesis assigns the lights the task of marking seasons, days, and years.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.1.16	lights made by God	The commentary's Abraham scene rejects stars, moon, and sun as rulers over their Maker; Genesis places the two great lights among the things God made and appointed to govern day and night.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Wis.13.1	failure to know the maker	The commentary calls each created kind a sign by which the Lord is known; Wisdom says people who infer no knowledge of God from visible good things fail to recognize their maker through his works.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Wis.13.3	beauty points beyond itself	The commentary says the worlds are signs that show their Lord; Wisdom argues that the beauty of created things should lead their observer to perceive the maker.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Wis.13.5	greatness of creatures	The commentary treats the whole creation as a field of divine signs; Wisdom says the greatness and beauty of creatures give a proportionate way to perceive their creator.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.1.20	invisible maker known through works	The commentary says creatures are signs by which their Lord is recognized; Paul says God's unseen power and divinity are perceived through what has been made.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rom.1.21	failure to glorify the maker	The commentary presents praise as the proper verdict on God; Paul describes people who knew God yet failed to glorify or thank him, showing the opposite response to creation's testimony.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rom.1.25	creation mistaken for God	The commentary's Abraham rejects a created light as Lord because it sets; Paul condemns exchanging the Creator's glory for worship of created things, including heavenly and earthly forms.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Job.31.26	sun and moon not worshiped	The commentary's Abraham refuses the setting sun and moon as possible lords; Job's speaker swears that seeing the bright sun or splendid moon did not turn him toward their worship.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Job.31.27	heart not enticed by lights	The commentary makes the refusal of celestial worship the test of who remains Lord; Job names the hidden temptation of the heart and the hand's kiss to the moon as forbidden worship.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Job.31.28	loyalty to God above	The commentary says the bodies that set are signs, not the enduring Lord; Job says such worship would deny God above and be a culpable offense.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.4.19	do not worship the host of heaven	The commentary identifies the sun, moon, and stars as created signs that cannot be Rabb; Moses warns Israel not to be drawn into worshiping those lights, which the Lord allotted to peoples under heaven.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Gen.15.5	stars as promise, not deity	The Qur'anic Abraham tests the star and rejects it when it sets; Genesis instead has God show Abram the stars as a measure of promised descendants, making the same sky a sign of God's word rather than an object of worship.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Gen.15.6	trust in the speaker	The commentary's Abraham turns from transient lights to their creator; in Genesis Abram responds to God's promise through the stars by trusting the speaker, not treating the stars as his lord.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.14.19	blessing God Most High	The commentary says hamd is the verdict that belongs to the doer of the praised work; Melchizedek blesses God Most High as maker of heaven and earth and as the one who delivered Abram's enemies.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.14.23	refusing human credit	The commentary rejects drawing praise to oneself for a good whose source lies elsewhere; Abram refuses the king of Sodom's goods so he cannot claim to have made Abram rich.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.8.10	bless after being satisfied	The commentary says hamd exceeds thanks for relief but still includes response to received good; Moses commands Israel to bless the Lord after eating and being satisfied.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Deut.8.17	wealth claimed as one's own	The commentary exposes the person who locates the source of a gift in himself; Moses warns against saying one's own power and strength acquired the wealth.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.8.18	God gives capacity	The commentary returns praise to the source of every good work; Moses says the Lord gives the power to produce wealth and thereby keeps the covenant.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Chr.29.11	heaven and earth belong to God	The commentary names Allah as the one to whom all praise belongs and Rabb of all worlds; David's prayer says greatness, power, glory, victory, and majesty are God's because all in heaven and earth is his.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Chr.29.13	thanksgiving to God's name	The commentary attaches praise to the one who did the work; David and the gathered people thank and praise God's glorious name after naming his universal kingdom.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Chr.29.14	nothing comes from ourselves	The commentary opposes human appropriation of credit for what was given; David asks what the people can give when everything comes from God and what they offer is already his.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.24.2	earth and fullness are God's	The commentary calls God the Rabb of all worlds; this psalm grounds the claim in God's ownership of the earth, its fullness, and its inhabitants.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.100.4	maker and pasture flock	The commentary's Rab imagery includes owner, herd, pasture, and the one who tends; the psalm says God made the people and calls them his flock, then brings them to worship with thanksgiving and praise.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.103.19	kingdom over all	The commentary stretches the limited human use of Rabb to the Lord of all worlds; this verse says God's throne is established in heaven and his kingdom rules over all.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.103.22	all works bless God	The commentary says the praise of creation is not produced by the human reader; the psalm summons all God's works, everywhere in his dominion, to bless him.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.145.10	all works give thanks	The commentary says every created kind knows its Lord through signs; this verse says all God's works give thanks while his faithful ones bless him.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.145.11	kingdom's glory proclaimed	The commentary identifies the Rabb of all worlds; the next line has worshipers speak of the glory and power of God's kingdom to make it known.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.145.16	God feeds every living thing	The commentary's Rab field includes nurture, water, pasture, and herds; the psalm says God opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.104.27	creatures depend on God's provision	The commentary links Rabb with the cloud that grows plants and sustains herds; this psalm says all creatures wait for God to give them food in its season.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.147.8	clouds bring rain and grass	The commentary develops the layered cloud that waters plants and pasture; this verse says God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on the mountains.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.147.9	food for cattle and birds	The commentary moves from cloud and water to the herd that remains where it is fed; this verse says God gives animals their food and feeds the young ravens.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.65.10	rain makes the land fruitful	The commentary joins the cloud that grows plants with hamd as a judgment that a place is good to inhabit; the psalm describes God watering furrows and softening the soil for grain.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.65.14	flocks and fields sing	The commentary brings Rab, abundant water, pasture, and a herd that stays together into one scene; this verse clothes the pastures with flocks and has valleys shout and sing.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.23.2	shepherd leads to water	The commentary's Rab branches include an owner and a herd, while its prose describes nurture as bringing a being toward completion; the psalm pictures the Lord as shepherd who gives pasture and still water.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.34.16	seeking the lost and injured	The commentary joins the owner of the herd with the lost animal and the nurturing Rabb; Ezekiel says God himself seeks the lost, brings back the strayed, binds the injured, and strengthens the weak.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.11.25	Lord of heaven and earth	The commentary couples praise with Rabb of all worlds; Jesus blesses the Father as Lord of heaven and earth, and the context says revelation is given to little ones rather than self-assured wise people.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.11.36	all things from and to God	The commentary returns every praiseworthy deed to its source and calls God Rabb of all worlds; Paul says all things are from, through, and toward God, to whom glory belongs forever.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Col.1.17	all things hold together	The commentary develops the image of the Rabb as the one who keeps a diverse plurality from scattering; Colossians says all things cohere in Christ, offering a Christian formulation of that sustaining relation.
medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:1Cor.4.7	received gifts exclude boasting	The commentary contrasts praise returned to its source with a person claiming a gift as his own; Paul asks what anyone has that was not received, and therefore why boast as if it were not received.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.9.23	boast in knowing the Lord	The commentary warns against pulling praise toward oneself; Jeremiah forbids boasting in wisdom, strength, or wealth and directs boasting toward understanding and knowing the Lord.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.27.2	another should praise you	The commentary criticizes the person who draws praise to himself for his own acts; Proverbs says praise should come from another's mouth, not one's own.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.1	piety done for human praise	The commentary opposes claiming credit and praise for oneself; Jesus warns against practicing righteousness in order to be seen by people, shifting recognition to the Father who sees in secret.
medium	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Luke.18.11	Pharisee's self-praising prayer	The commentary's false claimant wants praise for himself; in Jesus' parable the Pharisee's prayer thanks God but immediately boasts of his own virtue, while the following tax collector asks for mercy.
medium	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Luke.18.14	tax collector rather than self-exalting Pharisee	The commentary separates genuine praise from self-congratulation; Jesus says the humbled tax collector goes home justified, while the one exalting himself is brought low.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.19.1	praise after judgment	The commentary notes hamd after the unjust people's destruction as a verdict, not gratitude for a gift; Revelation's multitude gives glory and power to God after the judgment of Babylon.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.19.2	God's judgments are true and just	The commentary says hamd can approve the right outcome after a judgment; Revelation explicitly praises God because his judgments are true and just and he has judged the corrupting power.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.15.1	praise after an oppressor falls	The commentary's exact hamd formula follows the cutting off of a wicked people; Moses' song begins after Egypt's army is defeated and praises the Lord for triumph over the oppressor.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.98.7	sea roars before the judge	The commentary joins creation's praise with the final judgment that sets things right; this psalm has the sea roar before the Lord who comes to judge the world.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.98.8	rivers clap and hills sing	The commentary says nonhuman creation praises in ways people do not grasp; the rivers clap and hills sing before the Lord in the same scene that announces his righteous judgment.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.98.9	the Lord judges all the earth	The commentary's hamd after judgment is a verdict on what is right; this verse says the Lord comes to judge the earth with righteousness and the peoples with equity.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Chr.16.33	trees sing before the judge	The commentary says creation's praise is not a human performance; David's public worship song has the trees sing before the Lord because he comes to judge the earth.
medium	tevrat	motif	Mishnah, Berakhot 9:5	blessing in adversity	The commentary says hamd is a judgment broader than thanking someone for an advantage; the Mishnah requires a person to bless God for misfortune as for good fortune, making praise independent of immediate relief.
medium	tevrat	motif	Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 35a–b	blessing acknowledges the owner	The commentary says praise belongs to the source of every good rather than to the person who receives it; the Talmud treats enjoyment of the world without a blessing as misappropriating what belongs to God.
medium	tevrat	motif	Pirkei Avot 6:11	creation made for divine glory	The commentary says each created kind is a sign of its Lord and that praise is not dependent on a human speaker; this rabbinic saying gives the purpose of all creation as the Creator's glory.
medium	tevrat	motif	Adon Olam, opening and closing stanzas	Lord before and after creation	The commentary calls God Lord of all worlds and says the Lord remains when transient things pass; the hymn praises the Lord who precedes creation and reigns alone after all things cease.
medium	incil	motif	Augustine, Confessions 10.6.9–10	creation answers about its maker	The commentary says the worlds are signs through which the Lord is known; Augustine questions earth, sea, sky, sun, moon, and stars, and each directs him beyond itself to its maker.
medium	incil	motif	Song of the Three Youths, Greek Daniel 3:57–88	all works summoned to bless God	The commentary says every thing praises God in its own manner; this hymn lists works of creation and summons them to bless and exalt the Lord. Numbering differs across editions.
medium	tevrat	soydas	Mishnah, Avot 1:6	Hebrew rab as teacher or master	The commentary's Arabic dictionary glosses Rabb as owner, obeyed master, and one who sets things right; the Mishnah's Hebrew cognate rab is a human teacher one appoints, preserving the master-teacher sense without claiming it means Lord of all worlds.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.2.48	Aramaic rab as chief	The commentary glosses Rabb as owner and obeyed master; Daniel's Aramaic uses rab for a human chief set over other officials, a concrete cognate in a limited social relation.
medium	incil	soydas	SBLGNT:John.1.38	Rabbi glossed as teacher	The commentary includes master and nurturing teacher among the senses heard alongside Arabic Rabb; John's disciples address Jesus with the Semitic title Rabbi and the narrator explains it as Teacher.
weak	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.19.11	Hebrew cognate hmd means desirable	The commentary labels Arabic hamd from h-m-d as praise and a verdict of worth; the Hebrew cognate in this verse describes the Lord's instruction as desirable, a related evaluative sense rather than a word for praise.
EOF

medium	tevrat	motif	Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 35a	blessing before enjoying the world	The commentary says praise belongs to the source of what people receive; the Talmud treats a blessing as the acknowledgment that the world's enjoyment belongs first to God.

medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.26	birds fed by the Father	The commentary's Rabb imagery includes the owner and sustainer of a herd; Jesus points to birds that neither sow nor gather yet are fed by the heavenly Father.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.19.40	stones cry if people are silent	The commentary says praise is already located before a human reciter and does not depend on the reader's voice; Jesus says that if his disciples were silent, the stones would cry out.

strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.1.11	creation perishes, Lord remains	The commentary's Abraham rejects lights that set and its later passage says all on earth perishes while the Lord remains; Hebrews says the created heavens and earth wear out while the addressed Lord remains.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.1.12	unchanging through the end	The commentary's contrast is between passing worlds and the abiding Lord; Hebrews says creation will be changed like a garment while the Lord stays the same and his years do not fail.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.10.26	earth and fullness belong to the Lord	The commentary says all praise and every good belong to the creator rather than a human possessor; Paul quotes the psalmic claim that the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord while discussing food from the market.
medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rev.5.13	the Lamb shares cosmic praise	The ayah assigns all hamd to Allah; Revelation's universal doxology addresses blessing, honor, glory, and might to both the one on the throne and the Lamb, preserving a distinct Christian account of who receives cosmic praise.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.15	only Sovereign and King of kings	The commentary says Rabb without qualification belongs to the enduring Lord of all worlds; Paul calls God the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.16	immortality and honor	The commentary contrasts the setting lights with the Lord who remains; Paul says God alone has immortality and ascribes eternal honor and power to him.
EOF",
  workdir: "/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation",
  max_output_tokens: 1000
});
